CovalentFormer — A Covalent Medicinal Chemist Assistant

Qwen2.5-7B + LoRA over 585,530 rows — reaction chemistry, analogue design, and pocket-conditioned covalent hit-to-lead — with a Siamese ΔpIC50 head.

GLU166unmet carboxylate in S3OE2 is 4.56 Å from the nearest ligand N/OGrow a short donor off the P3 arm — one bond-length turns a near-miss into the canonical S3 hydrogen bond.
HIS163S1 anchor left unusedND1 4.70 Å from any ligand N/O, though the hit already carries a pyrrolidinoneReach it: shorten or re-angle the P1 arm so the lactam carbonyl meets ND1 — the move the shortened-linker lead makes.
ASN142 / SER144polar rim facing a carbonOD1 3.24 Å from ligand C21; SER144 OG unpartnered at 4.13 ÅSwap C21 for an acceptor — no growth needed. It relieves the mismatch and can pick up SER144.
PHE140unfilled lipophilic shelfsix side-chain carbons at 4.42–7.0 Å with no ligand carbon packed against themGrow a small lipophile in: methyl→cyclopropyl, or fuse a ring onto the P1 head.
C32 terminusvector into bulk solventthe most exposed ligand atom — only 6 protein atoms within 6 ÅGrow solubility here, or cut it. Properties, not potency.

The covalent bond is not on this list: CYS145 SG is 1.81 Å from ligand C25, the anchor the reaction frame is built on rather than a degree of freedom. ASN142 carries no arrow because it is a substitution at a position the ligand already occupies, not an extension.

shared core — crystal coordinates atoms the edit adds — modelled CYS145, covalent contact gained contact lost

Each lead is one real rung-3 training row: the Change, the Intent, the Warhead decision, the contacts it Gains and Loses, and the analogue SMILES — exactly the six fields the model must produce from the pocket and the hit. The ΔpIC50 shown is illustrative only, derived from the contact ledger to make the panel readable; it is not a model output, and the measured prediction from the potency head is pending.

How to read the columns. TC→input Tanimoto of the proposed molecule to the input — the human reference band is 0.680, and above it means the edit is too timid. scaffold fraction keeping the input's Bemis-Murcko scaffold; the reference keeps it by construction, so anything lower is scaffold drift. grounded fraction of named residues that exist in that pair's table — necessary, not sufficient, and it reads 1.000 on sentences chemists reject. attrib 1a every number in the sentence appears somewhere in the input table; attrib 1b every (residue, distance) pair co-occurs in one row — the “real distance, wrong residue” class, whose practical ceiling is the reference's 0.709. elem/dir vs OWN is reference-free: does the prose describe the edit the model actually made? sensible and reasoning are chemist columns — the share of proposals judged a plausible analogue, and the share a reviewer would put in front of a medicinal-chemistry audience.

Three results worth stating plainly. First, no arm beats the trivial baseline on selectivity. Naming the nearest residue in the contact table, with no parameters at all, scores 0.5625; the best arm reaches 0.537. Second, fine-tuning fixes the easy half and none of the hard half — validity and heavy-atom error are repaired everywhere (base models at 12.10 and 18.82 fall to ~3.2–3.8), while attribution never approaches its ceiling. Third, the think/answer schema trades attribution away: the unschema'd ether0 arm reaches 0.551 on attrib 1b while both schema arms sit at 0.330 and 0.183, below every ChemDFM and SmileyLlama arm.

The 165-case chemist panel — and what it overturned. External reviewers scored four arms side by side on 165 cases, letters reshuffled per case, three independent reviewers: 495 judgements per arm, 9,900 booleans, no missing slots. ChemDFM g3 wins the chemist axis — 23.0% reasoning against ~15% for all three ether0 arms, best-in-case 88 against 31–55, and edit identification 15 points clear. An earlier 48-judgement panel had put the ether0 arms at 39.6 / 35.4 / 29.2% and seemed to order them; at ten times the sample they are a dead heat at 15.8 / 14.7 / 15.4% and the absolute rates were inflated about twofold. That ordering was noise. What survived, and strengthened, is attribution: the chemists now agree with the computable attrib 1b that ether0 g2 (38.6%, 1b 0.551) beats schema B (34.3%, 0.330) beats schema A (21.2%, 0.183) — the think/answer schema costs attribution. The figure to carry, though, is that “none of the four” won 280 of 495 judgements — 57%: more than half the time a chemist saw four proposals and judged none worth showing an audience. Every difference between arms sits inside that fact.

The g4 labelling pass improves attribution per sentence by about 14% — not the doubling the raw rate suggests. Same models, same schema, same benchmark; only the labels change. attrib 1b goes from 0.290 to 0.594 for ChemDFM and from 0.330 to 0.693 for ether0 schema B, against a reference ceiling of 0.709. That metric is the “real distance, wrong residue” class six reviewers across five panels called the dominant failure, and no arm had previously passed 0.551 — so the ceiling was in the labels, not the architecture. It tracks the label sets themselves: the g4 pass scores 100% on “every cited distance exists in the table” and 78.6% on “(residue, distance) co-occur in one row” against g3’s 92.4% and 55.2%. attrib 1a is now 1.000 on both arms and over-35-word sentences fell from 12.2% to zero. Read 1b with its denominator, though: the g4 arms cite 1.5–1.6 distances per sentence against g3’s 2.8–2.9, so they have ~45% fewer chances to mis-attribute. Multiplied through, g4 delivers about 14% more correct anchors per sentence (0.835→0.956 and 0.927→1.053), not twice as many. The arms inherited the g4 labels’ terser style (26.5 against 33.3 words) along with their better attribution, and 1b should never be quoted without distances-per-sentence beside it. The cost is real and not free: TC→input leaves the human band (0.683→0.644 and 0.682→0.624), groundedness dips, and selectivity falls. The chemist columns on both g4 arms are not yet measured.

Invented chemistry is the number to worry about, and it is the most trustworthy one here. It asks whether the rationale asserts a contact, bond or interaction the table does not support — an absolute check against the input, so unlike reasoning it is not swayed by which arms sat beside it, and unlike attribution no scoring convention touches it. Two independent reviewer pools put ChemDFM g3+g4 at 42.0% (external, 450 judgements) and 38.9% (in-house, 144) — close enough to trust the figure. Across the ChemDFM family it falls 70.8 → 63.2 → 51.5 → 42.0, which is real progress and still means roughly two proposals in five invent chemistry that is not in the pocket. That, not the reasoning column, is what stands between these models and use. ‡ ether0 base’s 37.5% is vacuous in the same way as its 100% attribution: it cites no distances and names no residues, so there is nothing for it to invent.

◊ ChemDFM g3+g4 was panelled twice, and two tempting comparisons are invalid. In-house 48 items and external 150 (126 distinct after removing byte-identical repeats a reviewer caught — de-duplicating moves reasoning 35.8%→38.1%, so the distinct figures are the ones quoted). The arm scores 38.1% reasoning externally and 47.8% in-house, the first time those two pools have landed within 1.25× of each other rather than 2–3× apart — because this pair shared both the single-slot design and a stated convention for undecidable atom ownership. That convention is also why its attribution reads 68.8%: it instructs reviewers to score unresolvable ownership as correct, and on an earlier panel the same rule moved attribution from 16% to 50%. The in-house strict reading, ~46%, is the honest comparator to the 32–35% of the g3 and g4 rows. Likewise the reasoning figure cannot be set against g3’s 23.0% or g4’s 22.4%, which came from paired panels where arms sit beside one another. The one clean comparison is against ChemDFM base — also single-slot, also external — where 14.6%→38.1% is a genuine 2.6× on an identical instrument. Establishing whether g3+g4 beats either parent needs one paired panel holding all three under a single convention.

The external panel settles the g3-vs-g4 question: scaling did not help. The same reviewers, same rubric, 495 judgements per arm. ChemDFM reasoning is flat (23.0% → 22.4%) while its edit identification falls 66.9% → 54.3%; ether0 schema B drops on both (14.7% → 10.7% reasoning, 98.6% → 88.7% sensible). “Neither arm worth showing” rose from 57% to 67% of judgements. The one gain is ChemDFM inventing less chemistry (63.2% → 51.5%). And the automated attribution gain is invisible to chemists: attrib 1b doubled on both arms while chemist-judged attribution moved 32.1→34.7 and 34.3→31.5. g4 bought a metric, not a capability. ¤ marks the in-house 48-case panel, which runs 2–3× more generous than the external one on reasoning and must not be compared across the two scales.

The base models were panelled too, and the comparison is uncomfortable. 48 judgements per arm from the same external reviewers: untrained ChemDFM scores 14.6% on reasoning, while those reviewers scored fine-tuned ether0 schema B at 14.7%, schema A at 15.8% and ether0 g2 at 15.4%. Fine-tuning ether0 on these labels produced rationales chemists rate no better than an off-the-shelf ChemDFM given no training at all. Fine-tuning is not worthless — validity, heavy-atom error and groundedness all improve sharply — but the gain did not land on chemist-facing reasoning quality. One caveat on the base rows: all three base arms cite zero distances, so their attribution figures measure different things (ether0 base’s 100% is vacuous — nothing cited, nothing miscited), and that column must not be read across the base and trained rows.

Footnotes. ¶ the 165-case external panel, 495 judgements per arm — the numbers to quote. § the earlier 16-case, 48-judgement panel, retained only on the two 8B g3 rows that the larger panel did not cover; its absolute rates run about twice the 165-case ones, so § and ¶ must never be compared. † a different panel; panel-to-panel drift on these two columns is larger than most differences between arms, so only within-panel contrasts are meaningful. ‡ rides on a near-empty denominator: the base model cites almost no distances, so “the ones it cites are right” is close to vacuous. A 165-case, four-arm chemist panel and a 48-item base-model panel are out with external reviewers; they replace the § and TBD chemist cells with one consistent scale. The benchmark is used for model selection as well as reporting (val_is_model_selection_not_test), so these are not held-out test numbers.

3The three training phases

Each rung presupposes the last. Rung 1 teaches what a covalent reaction is; rung 2 teaches how to edit a molecule without breaking it; rung 3 asks for the real job — given a pocket and a covalent hit, propose a better covalent analogue and say why. A fourth channel, the potency head, spans rungs 2 and 3 and is the only part that emits a number rather than text. Each phase below is followed by its evaluation on the held-out test set, against the untuned base model and against Claude.

Phase 1 Covalent chemistry 373,935 rows · 63.9%

Four subtasks over covalent reactions, ligand-only. ADDUCT runs the reaction forward — given the electrophile and the attacking residue, write the adduct; RETRO inverts it, recovering the reactants from the product; SELECTIVITY names which residue is attacked, over six classes; WARHEAD_ID names the electrophile class, over ten. Two generative and two classification, which is the point: a model that can name a warhead but cannot form its adduct has learned vocabulary rather than chemistry, and the tables below show that gap directly. No pocket and no design decision — this rung teaches what a covalent reaction is, so the rungs above it can assume it.

Phase 1 evaluation — one table per subtask

Scored on 300 rows per subtask (1,200 generations per arm) drawn from the 32,082-row held-out fold, which is split by input molecule so no test molecule can reappear under a different subtask. Both arms get a byte-identical prompt, composed by the same function training used. For the generative subtasks, precision is the share of emitted SMILES that were correct and recall the share of asked rows answered correctly.

Phase 2 Analogue design · hit-to-lead 68,868 rows · 11.8%

Matched molecular pairs over covalent ligands. Given a hit, propose a close analogue that keeps the warhead and the binding scaffold — the two constraints that make an edit a medicinal-chemistry move rather than an arbitrary new molecule. The label names the transform before giving the SMILES, which turns open-ended generation into a decision that can be scored. Still no pocket: this rung teaches editing, not placement.

Phase 3 Covalent hit-to-lead, pocket-conditioned 3,015 unique · 2.1%

The target task, and the one shown in 3D at the top of this report. The hit arrives with its own co-crystal pocket, expressed in the covalent reaction frame: the attacked electrophilic atom at the origin, the attack axis as +z, and +x toward the Murcko-scaffold centroid. That frame is why the geometry generalises across complexes. The output is a full rationale: the structural Change, the Intent, the Warhead move, the contacts it Gains and Loses, and only then the Analogue.

Channel 4 The potency head130,667 rows · 22.3%

9Labelled dataset — 10 examples from covalent programmes

Real rows from the rung-3 labelled set, chosen for recognisable target proteins. Each was labelled by the same process as every other row: three independent medicinal-chemistry reviewers, then a chair who could adopt one of their sentences, write its own, or reject the row outright. The chair saw the measured geometry first and the proposals second. Orange marks the atoms that changed.

Rung 3 is v5 only: v4b's rung-3 label emits a one-word class (Intent: RECOGNITION) rather than a sentence, so it has no prose to show. Rows are ordered by similarity to mol1; all eight keep the acrylamide and carry the model's own sentence. Two partial-retention patterns run in opposite directions — rows badged isoindoline held keep the warhead's ring and swap the imidazole head, while the others keep the head intact and edit the ring. Read the sentences as fluent rather than uniformly faithful: several name groups mol1 does not carry (a tosyl, a tolyl cap, a terminal aldehyde). Where a row cites pocket residues they are real — 75 of 77 citations across the cohort, 97.4%, name a residue present in the prompt — but no generation in 600 both held the scaffold and reasoned from the pocket.

ΔpIC50 is read from each arm's own Siamese potency head and is ranking-grade, not calibration-grade: on the held-out fold v4b's head scored R² −0.209 globally — worse than predicting the mean on absolute error — while reaching Spearman 0.658 within a single hit's analogue series. Comparing these 600 analogues against each other is meaningful; the absolute values are not.
